items.title: Hakeem Jeffries supports impeaching Pete Hegseth, and a deadly mass shooting in Poland: Weekend Rundown
items.excerpt: Nov. 8, 2026, 6:00 PM EST By Mark Hodge, Amina Kilpatrick and Kayla Hayempour House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he supports efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week. Asked in an interview on ABC News’ “This Week” whether he would support Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in his efforts to impeach Hegseth, Jeffries confirmed he supported the push. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. Jeffries’ support is a major endorsement of the effort, and it signals how other House Democrats could ultimately vote. The push also tests how far lawmakers are willing to go to oust the top Defense Department official after voters gave low marks to the administration’s handling of the war in Iran, which was a factor in the midterm elections. ## Kraków shooting that killed 6 was motivated by far-right views, authorities say Poland has declared two days of national mourning after a shooter motivated by far-right ideology killed six people in Kraków on Saturday in what the country’s defense minister described as a “terror attack.” The gunman, whom officials described as holding “ultranationalistic” beliefs, reportedly opened fire in the city’s Main Market Square, killing four women and two men. A police officer who confronted him was among the 16 people injured and remains in critical condition. Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said the suspect is being investigated on suspicion of murdering six people. He said the attacker “acted with the aim of seriously intimidating a large number of people,” making the shooting a terrorist offense. The man, who was shot by police and remains in critical condition, is also being investigated in the deaths of three relatives found at his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 93 miles northeast of Kraków. ... ## Israel’s president taps opposition candidate to form a government ... Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27, a major blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a clear majority in the vote. In marathon discussions with Herzog this week, representatives from most of Israel’s main parties recommended that Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government. The announcement, which had been expected Sunday, came shortly after Netanyahu called for a “national unity government” in a video statement and warned against “hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters” — an apparent reference to the Arab-led parties. ## Nvidia opens investigation after reports CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence ... The board of Nvidia said Sunday that it was opening an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The announcement followed reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who the newspapers reported had been recruited to spy for China. The two are not related. In a memo to employees shared with NBC News, Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” The company added that while it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

items.title: US inflation set to cool in October after two months of sharp increases | World News - Business Standard
items.excerpt: Bloomberg 8 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 1:03 PM IST By Vince Golle and Craig Stirling Prices for US goods and services probably rose at a slower pace in October after two particularly uncomfortable months for American consumers. The consumer price index is seen rising 0.3% after a 0.6% increase that was the largest since April, based on the median projection in a Bloomberg survey of economists ahead of Tuesday’s Bureau of Labor Statistics’ release. The core measure, which excludes often-volatile energy and food components, also probably cooled. The survey median sees a 0.2% increase for October, which would be the smallest advance in three months. The agency won’t publish year-over-year figures after it skipped the October 2025 CPI release due to the federal government shutdown at the time. ## The Fed is expected to hold rates steady. Warsh will have to explain why ## Fed Chair Warsh stresses price stability, offers no signals on rate outlook The October CPI will be the last before the Federal Reserve’s meeting in December, at which investors expect policymakers to boost interest rates. Economists will also assess the finer details of the report for clues on inflation risks into early 2027. Economists at Citigroup Inc. said in a recent note that they anticipate limited pass-through of high energy costs to goods prices, as well as moderate services inflation. What Bloomberg Economics Says... > “We expect headline CPI slowed to 0.25% in October (vs. 0.65% prior). The core likely softened to 0.24% (vs. 0.33% prior), with both softer goods and services price gains driving the improvement. For goods, used cars and consumer electronics — categories that have faced pressure from the AI boom — saw slower inflation. For services, gains in owners’ equivalent rent are down a third from a September spike.” > > > > —Anna Wong, Troy Durie and Eliza Winger The latest snapshot of inflation also follows Friday’s stronger-than-expected October jobs report. Sustained employment growth has the potential of ensuring consumers keep spending, while allowing the Fed to keep its focus squarely on inflation. Another price report, due on Friday, is projected to show nagging inflationary pressures faced by companies. The producer price index is forecast to accelerate to 6.6% for the year through October, the steepest annual increase in nearly four years. Aside from inflation reports, National Association of Realtors figures on Thursday are expected to show a decline in contract closings on previously owned homes to the lowest level since 2010 as mortgage rates stay elevated.

items.title: US inflation, housing and jobs: 4 key economic updates to watch this week - The Times of India
items.excerpt: Edited by Shivanghi Payal / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 08, 2026, 14:27 IST ... The US economy faces another important week of data releases, with inflation, housing sales and unemployment figures likely to offer fresh insights into the financial pressures facing consumers and businesses. The focus comes as American households continue to deal with high prices of everyday essentials, from petrol to groceries. The latest updates follow the US midterm elections, in which Democrats swept Congress, a week ago. The economic situation has also been shaped by the war between the US and Iran, which began in February and cut global oil supplies. The resulting rise in energy costs added to inflationary pressures that were already high because of President Donald Trump's unpredictable tariff conflict with much of the world. Economists, investors and policymakers will be watching the upcoming numbers to assess how the war and tariffs continue to affect prices, the housing market and employment. ## US inflation: October CPI and PPI figures in focus The first major update will come on Tuesday, when the US releases its consumer price index (CPI) data for October. Economists expect inflation to rise to 3.9%, against 3.7% in September. The CPI tracks price movements across a broad range of goods and services. Inflation has remained above 3% since March, following the start of the US war with Iran in February. The conflict led to a sharp rise in energy prices, which pushed up petrol prices and shipping costs. Businesses will also get a fresh reading of their costs on Friday, when the October producer price index (PPI) is released. Unlike the CPI, the PPI measures price changes before goods and services reach consumers. The September PPI report had recorded its biggest increase since December 2022. It also showed how higher fuel costs, particularly for diesel, were feeding into shipping and warehousing expenses. However, crude prices fell sharply over the past week after the US midterm elections. Some believe Democrats, who routed President Donald Trump's GOP, will push to end the Iran conflict, which has sent energy prices soaring. ## US housing market: Home sales expected to remain weak The housing market will be another area of focus, with high property prices and rising interest rates continuing to weigh on homebuyers. The National Association of Realtors will release its October existing home sales report on Thursday. Economists expect the number of previously occupied homes sold to remain largely unchanged from September. The slowdown is not new. Home sales have remained close to an annual pace of 4 million since 2023, well below the historical average of around 5.2 million. Property prices have continued to rise despite the sluggish sales activity. Home prices have recorded annual increases for 39 consecutive months. At the same time, the average interest rate on a benchmark 30-year mortgage is hovering near its highest level in almost three years. Borrowing costs could remain high as the Federal Reserve considers another increase in its benchmark interest rate at its December meeting. The move would be aimed at cooling inflation, which has remained stubbornly high. ... The broader employment market has held up, with US employers adding 165,000 jobs in October. However, there are signs that workers are facing growing pressure. Wage increases have been slow and have not kept pace with inflation, leaving households struggling with the rising cost of living. items.title: PCE inflation accelerates to 3.6% as GDP growth beats estimates, jobless claims fall – Trade Talk Journal
items.excerpt: November 8, 2026 US inflation accelerated in September, while economic growth exceeded expectations in the third quarter and jobless claims remained near multi-decade lows, presenting the Federal Reserve with a challenging policy outlook. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the central bank’s preferred inflation gauge, increased 0.5% month-on-month on a seasonally adjusted basis, taking the annual rate to 3.6%, according to Commerce Department data released Thursday. The monthly increase matched the Dow Jones consensus forecast, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below expectations. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% from the previous month and 3.1% annually. Both readings were in line with economists’ forecasts. Fed officials generally view core inflation as a better indicator of longer-term price pressures, although they monitor both measures. Inflation remains significantly above the Fed’s 2% target, even as the economy continues to demonstrate resilience. ## Economic growth exceeds expectations The Commerce Department report showed that US gross domestic product increased at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, beating the 3.1% estimate and accelerating from 2.2% growth in the second quarter. Consumer spending, a key driver of the US economy, increased 0.5% in September, slightly below the 0.6% gain forecast by economists. Personal income rose 0.2%, compared with expectations for a 0.3% increase. The combination of firm economic growth and persistent inflation could make it harder for policymakers to justify easing monetary policy in the near term. The data arrived a day after the Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75%-4.00%. Officials have said they can assess incoming economic information before deciding on their next move, despite inflation remaining elevated. “The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that’s happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said. Thursday’s figures, however, suggest that policymakers may have more work to do to bring inflation under control while sustaining economic growth.

items.title: Week in politics: Democrats plan for the next Congress, Trump's new Chief of Staff
items.excerpt: RASCOE: Can you put this Democratic sweep into perspective? LIASSON: It's the biggest shift in power since the 1974 elections right after Watergate. There's still more than a dozen races in the House left to be called, but the Democrats could have as big as an 80-seat majority in the House next January. And in the Senate, they have 54 seats now, but Mississippi and Alaska are still left to be called, and that could end up being 56 seats. Democrats also won up and down the ballot in red states. Texas was the most dramatic example of that - the governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, state lawmakers. There are also six new Democratic state trifectas. That means that Democrats will control both legislative chambers and the governor's mansion in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Those are big states that are important for the 2028 presidential elections. ... RASCOE: So what happened to the voters who broke for Trump in 2024? LIASSON: Well, the Trump coalition fell apart and turned back to Democrats. The groups that had moved toward him in 2024 - Latinos were the biggest swing - moved back to the Democrats. White non-college voters, young Black men, especially in the once-solid Republican South, African American voters, who are angry like everyone else about the war and the economy, were particularly angry that the Supreme Court had weakened the Voting Rights Act and allowed Republicans to gerrymander away congressional districts long held by Black representatives. Those voters turned out in huge numbers, even better than in the 2024 presidential election. RASCOE: OK. So with the incoming Congress, what does the Democratic Caucus look like? And what are they saying that they will do? LIASSON: Well, yeah. You know, there was a lot made this year about left-wing candidates winning, and the Democratic Socialists of America did increase their numbers in the House from four to eight. But they were not the majority makers. The majority makers were centrist Democrats who won in red states and rural places. And Hakeem Jeffries, who's poised to be the next House speaker, said he expects the caucus to work together to try to find the, quote, "highest common denominator." And he has the gift of a big majority, so he won't be beholden to any one group inside the Democratic ranks the way Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson was because he only had a three-seat majority. Democrats say what they want to do is focus first on affordability, pass bills that will lower prices for Americans on housing, healthcare, food, gas - hope that Trump will sign them. Second priority is accountability. There are going to be a lot of investigations. Democrats want to tell a story about the connection between high prices and corruption. RASCOE: And how has the president been taking all of this? LIASSON: Well, Donald Trump says different things at different times, as he often does. But he has said he's willing to work with Democrats to make deals. But if they can't agree, he'll become Mr. Veto. But he's also done something that better communicates how he's planning to go forward. He promoted Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff. Miller is the deputy chief of staff now, and he has promoted the hardest of hard lines on any number of issues, primarily mass deportations. He believes in unchecked executive power. And by choosing Miller, Trump is showing that he is ready for a lot of confrontation with an opposition Congress.

items.title: Trump and his Justice Department stand defiant as Democrats ready an investigative blitz | PBS News
items.excerpt: Politics Nov 8, 2026 3:58 PM EST President Donald Trump and his Department of Justice are taking a combative stance toward Democrats after their election victories in the midterms, signaling intense conflict to come as lawmakers prepare aggressive investigations into the executive branch next year. Trump set the tone, declaring on social media that investigative requests already made by Democrats are "extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable." Attorney General Todd Blanche echoed the Republican president and said criminal investigations of Democrats are possible. "They are not allowed to just go around threatening existing members of the administration, to go around threatening companies, and that's what President Trump is extremely worried about and he should be," Blanche said as he and congressional Democrats appeared on the Sunday news shows to discuss the repercussions from last week's elections. Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, is preparing investigations into what he calls the "Trump crime family." He said Democrats are not going to be intimidated. "The days of us not fighting back are over," said Garcia, D-Calif. The early rhetoric sets up a showdown ahead that will likely define Trump's remaining two years in office and test the power of Congress to put a check on the White House. About 7 in 10 voters nationally say Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. Democrats have made clear that impeachment is an option. If there are people who have been "shortchanging the American people, screwing over the American people, or stealing from the American people, then they need to be held accountable in a manner consistent with Congress' role, constitutionally," said Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York. ## Some Democrats are worried about overreach But the investigative onslaught is also a source of tension for Democrats, with many warning that delivering on their central promise to voters — actions to lower the cost of living — must take precedence. Some fear their resounding wins Tuesday that have given them healthy majorities in the House and Senate will prove fleeting if conflict with Trump defines the agenda. Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat elected to the chamber from Kansas in 94 years, expressed skepticism about impeachment, saying his campaign was about trying to bring people together. He said he does not want the next two years to be spent "dividing our country further." "I'm not as interested in impeachment as setting up guardrails," Hamilton said. Still, Hamilton said he understands that some investigations are necessary, and Democrats "have to look at what's happened in Washington." Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, said he wants to hold Trump accountable, but warned there was only so much time. "We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump," Sanders said. "We've got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives." ## Jeffries casts doubt on working with Stephen Miller Jeffries, who is on the cusp of becoming the nation's first Black House speaker, was asked on election night about the prospects of working with Trump. He said he would be ready to work with the other side of the aisle "whenever and wherever possible to deliver real results." Jeffries on Sunday criticized Trump's choice of longtime adviser Stephen Miller to succeed Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, calling him an "awful choice" and cast doubt on the prospect of working with him. "There's not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we're committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people," he said. Democrats across the ideological spectrum have been critical of the appointment of Miller, an architect of Trump's mass deportation machine that became an issue in the midterm elections. Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll. Jeffries also said he supports a pending resolution from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Jeffries said Democrats would be discussing it when they return to the Capitol this week. "Hegseth has got to go," he said. "I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries said. Hegseth in a video dismissed the impeachment push as "all about the politics of personal destruction." He said it "won't work with me." ## New senators express skepticism about Schumer At least two new incoming Democratic senators expressed some reservations Sunday about Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who's expected to be reelected to his post after leading his party back to the majority. Hamilton said he's told Schumer, who is currently running unopposed, that he means no disrespect but that the New Yorker is a polarizing figure in Kansas and Hamilton is aiming for someone less divisive. "What I'd be looking for is a leader who can lead from the center, somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together," Hamilton said. "It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us." Hamilton said he wants to get to know the other Democratic senators better before he makes any recommendations. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, whom Schumer did not back in the Democratic primary, said he had been committed to Sen. Chris Van Hollen, but acknowledged that the Maryland Democrat does not appear to be running for the post. El-Sayed said he and Schumer, who put $67 million into El-Sayed's general election campaign, "figured out how to work together" after the primary.

'Godzilla Minus Zero' stomps to a record-setting $31.6 debut, clobbering 'The Cat in the Hat' NEW YORK (AP) — “Godzilla Minus Zero” stomped into movie theaters with a chart-topping $31.6 million over the weekend, scoring a record debut for a foreign-language film at the North American box office. Takashi Yamazaki‘s “Godzilla Minus One” sequel easily thrashed Warner Bros.' animated “The Cat in the Hat.” That film, featuring the voice of Bill Hader, opened with $20.5 million. Third place went to Angel Studios’ “Drummer Boy,” with $9.3 million on its opening weekend. The Oscar-contending “Wild Horse Nine” notched Martin McDonagh's best opening weekend, with $6 million. The weekend also saw the widest North American release for an Indian film. The Hindi epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” launched with $12.2 million domestically and $32 million in India. LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand's convictions this week for rape and sexual assault have renewed scrutiny on the BBC and other media employers that may have looked the other way. Brand, who gained fame while cultivating an outrageous persona, was convicted Thursday on multiple charges involving several women. The BBC has apologized for a culture that allowed his behavior to go unchecked. An internal probe followed a joint investigation by The Times and Channel 4, which aired accusations from women who said they were abused by Brand. Analysts argue that Brand's raunchy image acted as a shield, allowing his excesses to be overlooked by employers and the public, too. ... NEW YORK (AP) — Britney Spears' 2001 self-titled album ‘Britney' marked a pivotal moment in her career. At 19, she was already a global icon, transitioning from teen pop to a more mature sound. The album, certified quadruple platinum, showcased her evolution with hits like “I'm a Slave 4 U.” On Friday, Legacy Recordings releases the “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition).” It features five previously unreleased tracks and two new remixes. These songs add depth to her legacy, reflecting themes of autonomy and self-definition. Fans can revisit the album, exploring its impact and Spears’ journey from adolescence to adulthood. NEW YORK (AP) — Awkwafina has taken a surprising turn in her career by diving into the culinary world. Her new Apple TV series, “Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook,” follows her journey from a novice cook to opening her own restaurant. The show, premiering Friday, captures her learning experiences, from making stir-fry to mastering Peking duck. Awkwafina was born Nora Lum and comes from a family with a rich restaurant history. They opened the New York City eatery Lum's. Her journey reconnects her with her roots and honors her family. The series also highlights a trend of Asian Americans returning to the restaurant industry, defying their parents' expectations. NEW YORK (AP) — Siân Heder's follow-up to the best picture-winning “CODA” chronicles the disability rights pioneer Judy Heumann. Heumann died at the age of 75 in 2023 while Heder was developing the movie with her. She resolved to push on with the project to honor Heumann and try to bring some of her accessibility gains to the movie industry. Characters with disabilities remain extremely uncommon in Hollywood productions, and big-screen biopics like “Being Heumann” are even more seldom. “Being Heumann,” starring Ruth Madeley as Heumann, features the largest ensemble ever of performers with disabilities. SANTIAGO, Chile (AP) — Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio has died in Santiago, Chile, at 52. His family announced his death Friday on Instagram, citing health reasons but not specifying the cause. Lelio was known for his groundbreaking film “A Fantastic Woman,” which portrayed a transgender woman and won the Academy Award for best international film. It was Chile's second Oscar win.

items.excerpt: Pattinson and Hoult join the Bond screen tests: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult have been added to the list of actors who screen-tested for the next James Bond, according to Deadline, which says they joined Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner in the final screen tests. The Hollywood Reporter says Pattinson’s test took place in London on the weekend of 24 October, while he’s filming The Batman Part II, as I mentioned when it paused in October. Hoult plays Lex Luthor in DC’s Superman films. Both reports are unconfirmed, and there’s no timeline yet, although most expect a decision by the end of the year. The Sun has claimed that O’Connor has won the part, which NME has described as a rumour. It’s the first Bond film since Amazon bought the franchise’s creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025. Ramayana’s Diwali weekend: Nitesh Tiwari’s epic Ramayana: Part 1 had a big start in India, but its first Friday saw a 26% drop. According to Sacnilk, it took ₹48.05 crore net on Friday (about $5 million), taking its India net total to ₹112.90 crore (about $12 million), and its worldwide gross to ₹221.05 crore (about $23 million) after two days. The makers claimed that its opening day gross worldwide was ₹155 crore, against Sacnilk’s estimate of ₹127.5 crore. Hindi accounts for about 73.5% of its India net. The film is the first of a two-part retelling of the epic, with Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi and Yash, and Diwali weekend should show whether it can bounce back. I’ll bring you the full opening-weekend numbers tomorrow. Nollywood’s ₦1 billion streak: In Nigeria, Agbara Nla: The Return was number one for a fifth consecutive weekend, with ₦27.4 million (about $21,000) from 4,781 admissions, taking its total to ₦450.1 million (about $338,000) from 75,444 admissions and closing in on the all-time Nollywood top ten. Cinemas as a whole took about ₦130.7 million (about $98,000) over the weekend, and October ended with ₦1.19 billion (about $895,000), the 11th consecutive month above ₦1 billion since December 2025. The Far East: Tokyo’s winners: The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival closed on Wednesday, with the Tokyo Grand Prix going to Milcho Manchevski’s Sister Brother Manhole Cover, a co-production between North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Serbia, Albania, Italy and the UK, which comes with a $19,000 prize. Sun Xun’s animated feature Magic Atlas, a Singapore production, won the Special Jury Prize, and Argentina’s Lisandro Alonso took Best Director for Double Freedom. The Kurosawa Akira Award went to Iranian director Mohammad Rasoulof, whom I mentioned at the Cate Blanchett screening, and Japan’s Mipo O. The festival showed 204 films to 69,072 people.
